title: Saving Faith: Hebrews 11:1-3, 6
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson explores the nature of saving faith through Hebrews 11, examining how faith differs from mere knowledge of Christianity and demonstrating that faith pleases God more than perfect works. The speaker illustrates that both those who accomplish great things and those who suffer greatly can possess genuine saving faith, and teaches that faith involves both looking back to Christ's work on the cross and looking forward to His future promises.

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. For by it, the elders obtained a good testimony. By faith, we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God so that the things which are seen were not made of things which are visible. (Hebrews 11:1-3)

> But without faith, it is impossible to please him for he who comes to God must believe that he is and that he is a rewarder of those who diligently seek him. (Hebrews 11:6)

## The Historical Context of George Whitefield and Nathan Cole

In 1740, a Connecticut farmer by the name of Nathan Cole heard that George Whitfield was going to preach in a field nearby. Whitfield was an Anglican priest who was not accepted by the Anglican church. The idea of an itinerant preacher was unheard of and made people uncomfortable, so he often had to preach in fields because churches either would not allow him or could not contain the crowds.

Benjamin Franklin literally measured the distance that Whitfield's voice could be heard in Philadelphia and calculated that he could be heard and understood by 20,000 people, which was greater than the population of Philadelphia at the time. Such was the power of his preaching.

When Nathan Cole heard that Whitfield was coming, he dropped his work, mounted his horse, and rode as fast as he could to hear him preach. Cole later wrote that as Whitfield preached, he became deeply aware of his sin and his need for Christ. The preacher's voice was not what ultimately changed Cole; rather, God opened his heart to see his desperate condition and the sufficiency of Christ.

## The Difference Between Knowledge and Saving Faith

What had merely been facts about Christianity for Nathan Cole became a living reality to him. Cole had attended church his whole life, but it was through the preaching of the gospel by Whitfield that he came to understand it. This is the difference between mere knowledge and saving faith.

Many people know facts about the gospel, but saving faith occurs when the Holy Spirit persuades and enables a sinner to embrace Christ for salvation. I encourage you to read chapter 14 of our confession, which provides a great definition of saving faith.

## Why Hebrews 11 Is Included in Scripture

Hebrews 11 is arguably the most referred to chapter in the book of Hebrews and is the longest chapter. Yet there is a certain mystery about it because it seems somewhat superfluous—you could jump from the end of chapter 10 directly to chapter 12 without missing the information in chapter 11. So why is it here?

The epistle to the Hebrews was likely originally a sermon that was preached and then written down. Sermons are helpful when you have illustrations to apply what is being taught, and that is one reason chapter 11 exists.

Moreover, at the end of chapter 10, a verse from the Old Testament is quoted: "the just shall live by faith." This verse is quoted three times in the New Testament—twice by Paul and once by the author of Hebrews. Interestingly, each time it is quoted, a different part is emphasized: In Romans 1, it is the just; in Galatians 3, it is shall live; and here in Hebrews 10, it is by faith. Hebrews 11 then comes in to tell us how living by faith looks—what saving faith is.

The beauty of Hebrews 11 is that these are all struggling people. It is comforting to know that other people have struggled, even with their faith, and yet they are exalted as examples of saving faith.

## The Elders and God's Testimony

In verse two, the author of Hebrews says: "For by it, that's faith, the elders obtain a good testimony." The elders here are not ecclesiastical rulers or bishops, but rather the ancient ones—the forefathers of Hebrews 11. All those who have gone before us obtained a good testimony. Someone testified in their favor because of their saving faith in the Messiah of God.

While verse two does not tell us who testified in their favor, we find in verse five that it was God himself. It says: "By faith, Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death and was not found because God had taken him. For before he was taken, he had this testimony that he pleased God."

How did Enoch please God? Through faith. **Faith pleases God.** This is an encouraging thought to all of us. Though we fail often, we can still please God through faith in Jesus Christ.

## God Requires Faith, Not Perfection

God requires perfection. Not that we must be perfect, but He requires absolute perfection to have any fellowship with anything. But He has that in Christ. He only needs one perfect one, and that is Christ. Because of Christ, God is not primarily after perfection in us—He is after faith in us.

This is an important concept because we might often say we believe we are saved by grace, but then we end up living as if perfection is the basis of our relationship to God. We think, "Unless I am really good, unless I obey everything He says, then He does not love me." This chapter says no. It is faith that God requires from us.

We are saved through faith in Christ. We stay saved through faith in Christ, and we will be saved through faith in Christ. As important as obedience is in the life of a Christian, trust in Christ—looking back to what He did on the cross and, as we will see, looking forward to the promises of God—is infinitely more important than any work that you can do.

What God wants to know is: Do you believe in My Son now? Not yesterday, not tomorrow. Do you believe in My Son now?

## The Twenty Examples of Faith in Hebrews 11

Chapter 11 contains twenty examples of faith: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Moses' parents, Israel crossing the Red Sea, Jericho's conquest, Rahab, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets.

But the very first example of persevering faith is actually the Hebrew Christians themselves who are struggling with their faith at this very moment. Verse three says: "By faith we understand the worlds we're framed by the word of God so that the things which are seen were not made of the things that are visible."

Whoever wrote this includes himself with the recipients—these are people trying to decide: Should we remain with Christ or not? Is Christ worthy? Their faith was struggling; their faith was weak. But it was still faith in the Messiah. The Holy Spirit gave us this testimony so we would understand that these struggling people are believing in Jesus. The people who are struggling with believing in Jesus is the first example.

Some of these saints in chapter 11 did great things, and others suffered great things. And they are all holding the same faith in Jesus Christ.

## The Saints Who Did Great Things

Verse 33 says: "Who through faith subdued kingdoms. Worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, became valiant in battle, turned to flight the armies of the aliens. Women received their dead raised to life again."

How did they do that? By faith in Christ.

## The Saints Who Suffered

But look at the second half of verse 35: "Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. And still others had trial of mockings and scourges, yes, and of chains and imprisonment. They were stoned. They were sawn asunder. They were tempted. They were slain with the sword. They wandered about in sheep skins and goat skins being destitute, afflicted, tormented, of whom the world was not worthy. They wandered in deserts, mountains, and dens, and caves, and the earth."

Then verse 39: "And all these have obtained a good testimony through faith."

Do you see the greatness of this? It is not just the mighty, not just the Whitefields, the Spurgeons, the Susanna Wesleys—those whose names are recorded in history—who obtain the reward of faith. But those who are suffering, those who struggle, those who are barely holding on to Christ also receive the reward of faith.

It is not the quantity or the quality of our faith that matters. What matters is that we believe in the right Savior—the Lord Jesus Christ.

## The Nature of Faith: Definition

The nature of faith is given to us in verse one of chapter 11: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen."

It is important to realize that when verse one says faith is, it is not saying this is all that faith is. Faith is these things, but the Bible tells us more about what faith is. Faith is not less than what verse one tells us, but faith is more. Here, the Holy Spirit is emphasizing the elements of faith that fit the context of the church this letter was written to.

Faith is the substance of things hoped for. The word translated substance could also be translated essence or conviction. Faith is what undergirds hope. Faith brings what one day will be by sight and makes it a reality now.

By faith we know that one day we will be with Jesus face to face. By faith we know that He is coming back to us. By faith we know that we are going to be raised from the dead. Because we have faith, these things that we do not see become a reality for us now. They give essence to them. They give substance. Faith makes the promises of God, which are objectively real, real now for the ones who believe in them.

Faith is also the evidence of things not seen. You cannot see God. You cannot see heaven. You cannot see a life without sin. But by faith we believe that those things are real. They exist. They are our possibility and our reality. All we have is trust that what the Bible says is true. That faith is the proof that the things not seen are real, and faith will become sight.

## The Requirements of Faith

The author gives us requirements of faith in verse 6: "But without faith it is impossible to please him. For he who comes to God must believe that he is and that he is a rewarder of those who diligently seek him."

Without faith, you cannot please God. It does not matter how good you are. It does not matter what you do. Without faith, you cannot please God. He who has faith and accomplishes good works that could be done in a thousand lifetimes does not please God any more than the one who has faith alone.

Now faith is never alone—it always produces obedience to God's word. But it is the faith that is the instrument through which we secure God's favor, not what you do. Paul addresses this point in Romans 5, bringing everybody to look at the abyss of antinomianism—the idea that we do not have to obey anything; we just have to believe in Jesus. Then he pulls them back and says, "Oh yes, but faith that's real also obeys." But it is faith, brothers and sisters, not what we do.

Paul says in Romans 8:8, "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God." God is not going to be satisfied with anything that you do apart from faith in Jesus Christ.

There are two things regarding the content of faith that pleases God here in this verse. Remember that these are not exhaustive, but they assume an understanding of the backward-looking nature of faith that is so emphasized in Paul's writings.

First, one must believe in the historic work of Jesus Christ on the cross and the resurrection in order to please God.

Second, according to verse 6, we are to believe that God is who He says He is and that He will do what He says He will do. We are to believe in the promises of God because all promises, as Paul tells us in 2 Corinthians 1:20, are yes and amen in Jesus Christ.

This is the forward-looking aspect of faith that the author wanted to make clear to those people. God has not only acted in the past to bless His people; He will also act in the future. He has promised that Christ is coming back, and our faith grabs onto that and lives faithfully now.

So we look back and see the cross, but we also look forward and see the coming of Jesus Christ. That is why the Lord's Supper is so helpful. In the Lord's Supper, we remember that it was Christ who died for us. But also we do it in remembrance of Him until He comes back. We remember that He is coming back. We look backwards, and we look forwards, and in doing that, we stay faithful to Him as we serve Him.

## Can Struggling People Have This Kind of Faith?

Can struggling people really have this kind of faith? The author, by choosing these struggling Hebrew Christians as the first example of persevering faith, says yes. Even if your faith is weak, you still can persevere to the end.

Christ spoke often of His people as a smoking flax. The smoking flax is the wick of a lamp. When you blow a candle out, what happens? It smokes, right? That is what the smoking flax is—barely there, and yet it is there. That is all the faith that needs to be there.

He also speaks of His people as a bruised reed. That is a plant that has been bent, and it is good for nothing. It is bent but not broken. It is barely connected. That is the description of some of us, but we are still connected in Jesus Christ.

## Faith Must Include Belief in God's Creative Work

A key element for persevering faith is a firm belief that God created all things by the power of His word. Look at verse 3: "By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God."

Notice that all matters of origin are matters of faith. Did God create all things? It seems logical that things have not been around forever. Science points to the fact that things have not been around forever. Our daily experience points to the fact that things have not been around forever. By any measure, it is a matter of God-given faith that we know that God created all things. Why is it a matter of faith? Because we were not there. So we have to believe what we are told.

And that is true of science as well, right? Because nobody has been there. So either view—whatever view we have of origin—is a matter of faith.

Here it says that an element of true faith is that you believe that God made all things. It says the worlds, meaning the ages. Everything, time itself was made by God, and He made it out of nothing, the Holy Spirit tells us.

People say, "Oh, it is not important what you believe concerning creation as long as you believe that God created." But whoever wrote this—the Holy Spirit—says no. An element of faith is that you believe that God created all things out of nothing. That is what He did. He spoke, and there it was.

Now, there are people who have misguided beliefs concerning creation. This does not mean that they are going to hell for it, but it is a dangerous place to be because it is not faith in what the scriptures teach.

## Living by Faith: Grabbing Hold of God's Promises

So what do we do with what the author of Hebrews teaches us about faith? We grab hold of God's promises by faith and live by faith today because we will be able to live by sight tomorrow.

Just think about the promises that God makes in the Bible that are yours by faith:

**To die is gain.** Do you believe that dying is gain? It is a promise that God has made to us: "To live is Christ, to die is gain."

**To be with the Lord is far better.** That is another promise. Do you believe that?

**I am coming again for you.** The Lord says this. Do you believe that?

**I will be a very present helper in times of need.** We read Psalm 46 in Sunday school this morning. Whatever we are going through right now, this is true.

**I will never leave nor forsake you.** Whatever we are going through right now, this is true. Do you hold on to that promise?

**Delight yourself in the Lord, and I will give you the desires of your heart.** The reward of those who seek Him is the joy of finding Him. That is the desire that we get. Do you hold on to that promise?

And one last promise. This is from the book of Revelation. John speaks: "Then I, John, saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying, 'Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people. God Himself will be with them and be their God. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain for the former things have passed away.'"

Do you believe that? Do you believe that there will be pain until all things are made new? And do you believe that God is going to remove all that at His return? These are promises that are ours. They are true. They are objectively true, but faith gives substance to them. We claim them, and we hold on for them.

Why is it okay to suffer now? Because we will not suffer then.

Why is it okay to be mistreated now? Because we will not be mistreated then.

Why is it okay to be alone now? Because God will be forever with us for eternity.

We look back to the cross, but we also look forward to the coming of Christ as a motivator for us to keep on going.
